why: B127 (SSPN-294). An expression-bodied arrow is a function whose body is one expression: `const concise = () => g()` calls `g` exactly as `const block = () => { g(); }` does. The call walk started at the body's children, so a concise body that IS the call was never seen and `concise` drew no edge. Labelled from the source: every arrow here calls what its body calls, `nested` calls both `g` and `h` (the argument call was found all along, the outer one was not), and `shadow`'s parameter hides the file-level `g`, so it is a refusal, the control that a fix reading concise bodies keeps the shadowing rule.

refusals.why: PREDICTED BEFORE SCORING. `shadow`'s parameter `g` hides the module-level function; the concise body `g()` calls whatever the caller passes. The block form has refused this since the shadowing fix; a concise body must refuse it the same way.

excluded: `block` is NOT excluded: the block-bodied twin of `concise`, drawn before B127 and after. It is the control that the fix changes concise bodies only.
resolved_by_measurement: Written BEFORE the fix and scored on develop b9f0c891: `concise -> g` and `nested -> g` missed (CALLS recall 2 of 4 for this case); `nested -> h` and `block -> g` matched; the refusal held.
